L617: ### Resize mode
L618: 
L619: Depending on the 【72†WindowStyle】 property, you can control if, and how, users resize the window. The window style affects the following:
L620: 
L621:   * Allow or disallow resizing by dragging the window border with the mouse.
L622:   * Whether the Minimize, Maximize, and Close buttons appear on the non-client area.
L623:   * Whether the Minimize, Maximize, and Close buttons are enabled.
L624: You can configure how a window resizes by setting its 【73†ResizeMode】 property, which can be one of the following 【74†ResizeMode】 enumeration values:
L625: 
L626:   * 【75†NoResize】
L627:   * 【76†CanMinimize】
L628:   * 【77†CanResize】 (default)
L629:   * 【78†CanResizeWithGrip】
L630: As with 【72†WindowStyle】, the resize mode of a window is unlikely to change during its lifetime, which means that you'll most likely set it from XAML markup.
L631: 
L632:     `<Window
L633:         xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L634:         ResizeMode="CanResizeWithGrip">
L635:     </Window>
L636:     `
L637: 
L638: Note that you can detect whether a window is maximized, minimized, or restored by inspecting the 【64†WindowState】 property.
L639: ### Window style
L640: 
L641: The border that is exposed from the non-client area of a window is suitable for most applications. However, there are circumstances where different types of borders are needed, or no borders are needed at all, depending on the type of window.
L642: 
L643: To control what type of border a window gets, you set its 【72†WindowStyle】 property with one of the following values of the 【79†WindowStyle】 enumeration:
L644:   * 【80†None】
L645:   * 【81†SingleBorderWindow】 (default)
L646:   * 【82†ThreeDBorderWindow】
L647:   * 【83†ToolWindow】
L648: 
L649: The effect of applying a window style is illustrated in the following image:
L650: 
L651: 【84†Image: Screenshot that shows how WindowStyle affects a window in WPF.】
L652: Notice that the image above doesn't show any noticeable difference between `SingleBorderWindow` and `ThreeDBorderWindow`. Back in Windows XP, `ThreeDBorderWindow` did affect how the window was drawn, adding a 3D border to the client area. Starting with Windows 7, the differences between the two styles are minimal.
L653: You can set 【72†WindowStyle】 using either XAML markup or code. Because it's unlikely to change during the lifetime of a window, you'll most likely configure it using XAML markup.
L654: 
L655:     `<Window
L656:         xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L657:         WindowStyle="ToolWindow">
L658:     </Window>
L659:     `
L660: #### Non-rectangular window style
L661: 
L662: There are also situations where the border styles that 【72†WindowStyle】 allows you to have aren't sufficient. For example, you may want to create an application with a non-rectangular border, like Microsoft Windows Media Player uses.
L663: 
L664: For example, consider the speech bubble window shown in the following image:
L665: 
L666: 【85†Image: Screenshot of a WPF window that has a clipped area and custom shape.】
L667: This type of window can be created by setting the 【72†WindowStyle】 property to 【80†None】, and by using special support that 【5†Window】 has for transparency.
L668: 
L669:     `<Window x:Class="WindowsOverview.ClippedWindow"
L670:             xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L671:             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
L672:             Title="ClippedWindow" SizeToContent="WidthAndHeight"
L673:             WindowStyle="None" AllowsTransparency="True" Background="Transparent">
L674:         <Grid Margin="20">
L675:             <Grid.RowDefinitions>
L676:                 <RowDefinition Height="*"/>
L677:                 <RowDefinition Height="20"/>
L678:             </Grid.RowDefinitions>
L679: 
L680:             <Rectangle Stroke="#FF000000" RadiusX="10" RadiusY="10"/>
L681:             <Path Fill="White" Stretch="Fill" Stroke="#FF000000" HorizontalAlignment="Left" Margin="15,-5.597,0,-0.003" Width="30" Grid.Row="1" Data="M22.166642,154.45381 L29.999666,187.66699 40.791059,154.54395"/>
L682:             <Rectangle Fill="White" RadiusX="10" RadiusY="10" Margin="1"/>
L683: 
L684:             <TextBlock HorizontalAlignment="Left" VerticalAlignment="Center" FontSize="25" Text="Greetings!" TextWrapping="Wrap" Margin="5,5,50,5"/>
L685:             <Button HorizontalAlignment="Right" VerticalAlignment="Top" Background="Transparent" BorderBrush="{x:Null}" Foreground="Red" Content="❌" FontSize="15" />
L686: 
L687:             <Grid.Effect>
L688:                 <DropShadowEffect BlurRadius="10" ShadowDepth="3" Color="LightBlue"/>
L689:             </Grid.Effect>
L690:         </Grid>
L691:     </Window>
L692:     `
L693: This combination of values instructs the window to render transparent. In this state, the window's non-client area adornment buttons can't be used and you need to provide your own.
L694: ### Task bar presence
L695: The default appearance of a window includes a taskbar button. Some types of windows don't have a task bar button, such as message boxes, 【17†dialog boxes】, or windows with the 【72†WindowStyle】 property set to 【83†ToolWindow】. You can control whether the task bar button for a window is shown by setting the 【65†ShowInTaskbar】 property, which is `true` by default.
L696: 
L697:     `<Window
L698:         xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L699:         ShowInTaskbar="False">
L700:     </Window>
L701:     `
L702: ## Other types of windows
L703: 
L704: 【86†NavigationWindow】 is a window that is designed to host navigable content.
L705: 
L706: Dialog boxes are windows that are often used to gather information from a user to complete a function. For example, when a user wants to open a file, the Open File dialog box is displayed by an application to get the file name from the user. For more information, see 【17†Dialog Boxes Overview】.
L707: ## See also

L27: # Windowing overview for WinUI 3 and Windows App SDK
L28: 
L29:   * Applies to: ✅ 【5†WinUI】, ✅ 【6†Windows App SDK】
L30: 
L31: Feedback
L32: 
L33: Summarize this article for me
L34: ## In this article
L35: 
L36: Windowing functionality in a WinUI app is provided by a combination of the XAML 【7†Window】 class and the 【8†AppWindow】 class, both of which are based on the 【9†Win32 HWND model】.
L37: 
L38:   * Important APIs: 【7†Window class】, 【8†AppWindow class】
L39: 
L40: Open the WinUI 3 Gallery app and see Windowing samples in action
L41: 
L42: Open the WinUI 3 Gallery app and see Window in action
L43: > 【10†Image: WinUI 3 Gallery icon】  | The WinUI 3 Gallery app includes interactive examples of WinUI controls and features. Get the app from the 【11†Microsoft Store†apps.microsoft.com】 or browse the source code on 【12†GitHub†github.com】.
L44: 
L45: XAML Window
L46: In your app, the window object is an instance of the 【7†Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Window】 class (or a derived class) that represents the window in your program code. You create it directly with a call to the constructor. The XAML Window is where you attach your app content and manage the lifecycle of your app's windows.
L47: 
L48: HWND
L49: The application window is created by the Windows operating system and is represented by a Win32 window object. It's a system-managed container in which your content is hosted, and represents the entity that users interact with when they resize and move your app on-screen. (See 【9†About Windows】 in the Win32 documentation for more info.)
L50: After Windows creates the application window, the creation function returns a window handle (`HWND`) that uniquely identifies the window. A window handle has the HWND data type, although it's surfaced in C# as an 【13†IntPtr】. It's an opaque handle to an internal Windows data structure that corresponds to a window that's drawn by the OS and consumes system resources when present.
L51: 
L52: The HWND is created after the XAML 【7†Window】 object, typically when the 【14†Window.Activate】 method is called.
L53: 
L54: AppWindow
L55: The Windows App SDK provides additional windowing functionality through the 【8†Microsoft.UI.Windowing.AppWindow】 class. AppWindow represents a high-level abstraction of the HWND. There's a 1:1 mapping between an AppWindow and a top-level HWND in your app. AppWindow and its related classes provide APIs that let you manage many aspects of your app's top-level windows without the need to access the HWND directly.
L56: The lifetime of an 【8†AppWindow】 object and an HWND is the same—the AppWindow is available immediately after the window has been created; and it's destroyed when the window is closed.
L57: 
L58: Windowing API diagram
L59: This diagram shows the relationship between the classes and APIs that you use to manage windows in your app, and which classes are responsible for each part of window management. In some cases, like `ExtendsContentIntoTitleBar`, the API is a member of 【8†AppWindow】 to make it available to other UI frameworks, but is also exposed on the 【7†Window】 class for convenience. The diagram is not comprehensive, but shows the most commonly used APIs.
L60: 
L61: Note
L62: You can use 【8†AppWindow】 APIs with any UI framework that the Windows App SDK supports - Win32, WPF, WinForms, or WinUI. For frameworks other than WinUI, the functionality shown in the XAML Window box of the diagram would be replaced by the appropriate framework-specific windowing APIs:
L63: 
L64:   * 【15†WPF Window】
L65:   * 【16†Windows Forms Form】
L66:   * 【17†Win32 windowing APIs】, 【18†MFC Windows】
L67: ## Window/AppWindow API comparison
L68: 
L69: If you use WinUI XAML as your app's UI framework, both the 【7†Window】 and the 【8†AppWindow】 APIs are available to you. Starting in Windows App SDK 1.4, you can use the 【19†Window.AppWindow】 property to get an AppWindow object from an existing XAML window. With this AppWindow object you have access to the additional window management APIs.
L70: 
L71: Important
L72: If you're not using Windows App SDK 1.4 or later, use interop APIs to get the AppWindow in order to use the AppWindow APIs. For more about the interop APIs, see 【20†Manage app windows - UI framework and HWND interop】 and the 【21†Windowing gallery sample†github.com】.
L73: ### Lifetime management
L74: 
L75: The 【14†Window.Activate】 method attempts to activate the application window. If the calling app is in the foreground, the window is brought to the foreground (top of Z-order) and receives input focus. If the app is in the background, this method does not force the window into the foreground.
L76: XAML Window  | AppWindow
L77: --- | ---
L78: 【22†Constructor】  | 【23†Create】, 【24†GetFromWindowId】
L79: 【14†Activate】  | 【25†Show】, 【26†Hide】
L80: 【27†Close】, 【28†Closed】  | 【29†Destroy】, 【30†Destroying】, 【31†Closing】
L81: >>>  | 【32†Id】, 【33†OwnerWindowId】
L82: When you create a new WinUI project in Visual Studio, the project template provides a `MainWindow` class for you, which is a sub-class of 【7†Window】. If your app only needs one window, this is all you need. To learn how to create and manage additional windows, and why you might want to, see 【34†Show multiple windows for your app】.

L6: # Restoring from backup【1†】
L7: ## Restoring from a snapshot【2†】
L8: 
L9: Restoring a snapshot is as easy as it sounds, just use the following command to restore the contents of the latest snapshot to `/tmp/restore`:
L10: 
L11:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo restore 79766175 --target /tmp/restore
L12:     enter password for repository:
L13:     restoring snapshot of [/home/user/work] at 2015-05-08 21:40:19.884408621 +0200 CEST to /tmp/restore
L14: Use the word `latest` to restore the latest snapshot. You can also combine `latest` with the `--host` and `--path` filters to choose the latest snapshot for a specific host, path or both:
L15: 
L16:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo restore latest --path /home/art --host luigi --target /tmp/restore
L17:     enter password for repository:
L18:     restoring snapshot of [/home/art,/home/documents] at 2015-05-08 21:45:17.884408621 +0200 CEST to /tmp/restore
L19: Note that the `--path` option is only used to select the snapshot to restore, not to restrict the restore to a subset of files in the snapshot. This means that here the files will be restored to `/tmp/restore/home/art` and `/tmp/restore/home/documents`.
L20: Use either `--exclude` or `--include` to restrict the restore to a subset of files in the snapshot (the two are mutually exclusive). For example, to restore a single file:
L21: 
L22:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo restore 79766175 --target /tmp/restore --include /home/user/work/foo
L23:     enter password for repository:
L24:     restoring snapshot of [/home/user/work] at 2015-05-08 21:40:19.884408621 +0200 CEST to /tmp/restore
L25: 
L26: 
L27: This will restore the file to `/tmp/restore/home/user/work/foo`.
L28: To only restore a specific subfolder, you can use the `<snapshot>:<subfolder>` syntax, where `snapshot` is the ID of a snapshot (or the string `latest`) and `subfolder` is a path within the snapshot tree as shown by `restic ls`. Note that the subfolder syntax also affects options like `--include` and `--exclude`, such that their arguments should be specified relative to `subfolder` (e.g. `/foo` instead of `/home/user/work/foo`).
L29:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo restore 79766175:/home/user/work --target /tmp/restore --include /foo
L30:     enter password for repository:
L31:     restoring snapshot of [/home/user/work] at 2015-05-08 21:40:19.884408621 +0200 CEST to /tmp/restore
L32: This will restore the file `/home/user/work/foo` to `/tmp/restore/foo`.
L33: 
L34: You can use the command `restic ls latest` or `restic find foo` to find the path to the file within the snapshot. Pass that path to `--include` verbatim when restoring the full snapshot; with `<snapshot>:<subfolder>`, use a path relative to `subfolder` as in the example above.
L35: There are case-insensitive variants of `--exclude` and `--include` called `--iexclude` and `--iinclude`. These options will behave the same way but ignore the casing of paths.
L36: 
L37: There are also `--include-file`, `--exclude-file`, `--iinclude-file` and `--iexclude-file` flags that read the include and exclude patterns from a file.
L38: Restoring symbolic links on Windows is only possible when the user has the `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` privilege or is running as administrator. This is a restriction of Windows, not restic.
L39: Restoring full security descriptors on Windows is only possible when the user has the `SeRestorePrivilege`, `SeSecurityPrivilege` and `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege` privileges or is running as administrator. This is a restriction of Windows, not restic. If not all of these privileges are available, only the DACL is restored.
L40: By default, restic does not restore files as sparse. Use `restore --sparse` to enable the creation of sparse files if supported by the filesystem. Then restic will restore long runs of zero bytes as holes in the corresponding files. Reading from a hole returns the original zero bytes, but it does not consume disk space. Note that the exact location of the holes can differ from those in the original file, as their location is determined while restoring and is not stored explicitly.
L41: ### Restoring extended file attributes【3†】
L42: 
L43: By default, all extended attributes for files are restored.
L44: Use either `--exclude-xattr` or `--include-xattr` (not both) to control which extended attributes are restored for files in the snapshot. For example, to restore user and security namespaced extended attributes for files:
L45: 
L46:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo restore 79766175 --target /tmp/restore --include-xattr user.* --include-xattr security.*
L47:     enter password for repository:
L48:     restoring snapshot of [/home/user/work] at 2015-05-08 21:40:19.884408621 +0200 CEST to /tmp/restore
L49: ### Restoring in-place【4†】
L50: 
L51: Note
L52: 
L53: Restoring data in-place can leave files in a partially restored state if the `restore` operation is interrupted. To ensure you can revert back to the previous state, create a current `backup` before restoring a different snapshot.
L54: 
L55: By default, the `restore` command overwrites already existing files at the target directory. This behavior can be configured via the `--overwrite` option. The following values are supported:
L56:   * `--overwrite always` (default): always overwrites already existing files. `restore` will verify the existing file content and only restore mismatching parts to minimize downloads. Updates the metadata of all files.
L57: 
L58:   * `--overwrite if-changed`: like the previous case, but speeds up the file content check by assuming that files with matching size and modification time (mtime) are already up to date. In case of a mismatch, the full file content is verified. Updates the metadata of all files.
L59:   * `--overwrite if-newer`: only overwrite existing files if the file in the snapshot has a newer modification time (mtime).
